Furthermore, some stakeholders have expressed uncertainty regarding SAF performance under conditions (such as high altitudes or rapid maneuvers) that military aircraft may encounter at the extremes of their operating capability which have not yet been fully tested and certified. In addition, the International Civil Aviation Organization (ICAO) established a global framework for the regulation of international alignment around SAF (ICAO 2018; ICAO n.d.-b.). Regardless of nations potentially adopting higher-blend targets, those blends would need to meet international requirements and approval. Boeing approved the use of SAF in military aircraft with military fuels such as JP-8/NATO F-34 at blends of up to 50% (Boeing 2024). In 2025, Lockheed Martin approved the use of synthetic aviation turbine fuels in the F-35 Lightening II at blends of up to 50% based on “comprehensive 83 This report is available at no cost from the National Laboratory of the Rockies (NLR) at www.nlr.gov/publications. technical and strategic analysis to ensure that synthetic aviation turbine fuel meets the strict performance and reliability standards required for the F-35’s complex, high-demand missions” (Lockheed Martin 2025). Also in 2025, Norway tested the F-35 stealth fighter using 40% SAF/biofuels (Hoyle 2025). Researchers are working to achieve blends of SAF up to 100% with the necessary properties to ensure engine performance and safety. One possibility involves mixing two types of SAF with different properties, including one with aromatics from nonpetroleum sources. National Laboratory of the Rockies (NLR) experts estimate achieving 100% SAF could take 10 years with sufficient research and development funding and an internationally collaborative effort. New progress includes efforts by NLR in collaboration with the Massachusetts Institute of Technology in developing SAF that contains aromatics using plant lignin (Ringle 2025). The use of 100% drop-in SAF probably presents little technical risk to DOW, because DOW involvement in setting SAF requirements and blends at ASTM could prevent changes that risk fuel incompatibility with the current aircraft fleet. However, DOW may face higher costs for refueling where SAF blends are mandatory because SAF costs two to three times more than conventional aviation fuel (Parolini 2025, Primrose 2025). Demand (and therefore prices) will rise in part due to E.U. mandates for aviation fuel suppliers to provide minimum SAF blends to E.U. airports starting at 2% in 2025 and increasing to 70% in 2050, and United Kingdom mandates for a 2% SAF minimum in 2025 increasing to 22% in 2040 (EASA 2025). E.U. subsidies for airlines purchasing SAF will also encourage use (Abnett 2025b). As of June 2025, 17 additional countries have declared or proposed targets or mandates (including Japan, South Korea, and Turkey), or are otherwise developing policies (including China, the Philippines, Saudi Arabia) (Williams and Keane 2025). Because domestic SAF production capacity does not meet current demand (Rosales Calderon 2024b), any requirement for DOW to use SAF could pose a supply risk.
